title: Medical Certificates (Classes & BasicMed)

required_knowledge_points.title: Medical Certificate Classes & Durations
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot who confuses medical class durations may fly with an expired medical, creating both a legal violation and an undetected medical risk.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: The FAA issues three classes of medical certificates. First-Class is required for ATP operations (12 months under 40, 6 months 40+). Second-Class is required for commercial operations (12 months regardless of age). Third-Class is required for private, recreational, and student operations (60 months under 40, 24 months 40+). All durations use the calendar month rule — validity extends to the END of the expiration month. A First-Class medical does not expire completely; it steps down to lower privileges automatically. A 35-year-old with a First-Class issued January 1, 2024 can fly ATP through January 31, 2025, then private through January 31, 2029.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### First-Class Medical
- Required for **ATP operations**
- Valid **12 months** if pilot was **under age 40** at exam
- Valid **6 months** if pilot was **age 40 or older** at exam

### Second-Class Medical
- Required for **commercial pilot operations**
- Valid **12 months** regardless of age

### Third-Class Medical
- Required for **private, recreational, and student** operations
- Valid **60 months** if pilot was **under age 40** at exam
- Valid **24 months** if pilot was **age 40 or older** at exam

### Step-Down Rule (14 CFR 61.23)
- A **First-Class** does not expire completely — it **steps down** to lower privileges
- Example: A **35-year-old** with First-Class issued Jan 1, 2024:
  - ATP privileges valid through **Jan 31, 2025**
  - Private privileges valid through **Jan 31, 2029** (same certificate)
- Validity always extends to the **end of the calendar month** — not the exact date

required_knowledge_points.title: Self-Grounding & Temporary Disqualifications
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot who flies while taking disqualifying medication or with a known medical condition may be legal on paper but incapacitated in the cockpit.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: 14 CFR 61.53 is the self-grounding rule. A pilot is prohibited from acting as PIC if they know or have reason to know of any medical condition that would make them unable to meet the requirements for their medical certificate — even if the certificate is still valid. This includes taking disqualifying medications such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl), certain antidepressants, or sedatives. The FAA maintains a Do Not Issue / Do Not Fly medication list. The standard is based on the treatment itself, not the pilot's subjective feeling of wellness. The general withdrawal period is 5 times the half-life of the drug.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Self-Grounding Rule (14 CFR 61.53)
- Prohibited from acting as **PIC** if you **know or have reason to know** of any medical condition preventing you from meeting certificate requirements
- Applies even if your medical certificate is **currently valid**
- Standard is based on the **condition or treatment** — not how the pilot subjectively feels

### Disqualifying Medications
- FAA maintains a **Do Not Issue / Do Not Fly** medication list
- Examples: **diphenhydramine (Benadryl)**, certain **antidepressants**, **sedatives**, **opioids**
- Feeling "fine" on a medication does **not** make flight legal
- General safe waiting period: **5 times the drug's half-life** before flying

### Key Principle
- A valid medical in your wallet does **not** override your obligation to self-ground
- Developing a serious illness on the day of flight = **no-go**, regardless of certificate status

required_knowledge_points.title: Required Pilot Documents (The Big Three)
required_knowledge_points.why: Failure to carry required documents during a ramp check results in a violation and potential certificate action, even if the pilot is otherwise fully qualified.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: 14 CFR 61.3 requires a pilot to have three documents in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft: (1) a valid pilot certificate (plastic card only — paper certificates are no longer valid), (2) a valid government-issued photo ID (driver's license, passport, military ID, or TSA credential), and (3) a valid medical certificate or BasicMed course completion certificate. A logbook is NOT required to be carried during flight, though the pilot must be able to produce it upon request within a reasonable time. An expired driver's license means the pilot cannot legally fly, even with a valid pilot certificate and medical.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Big Three — Required Per 14 CFR 61.3
- **Valid pilot certificate** — plastic card only; paper certificates are **no longer valid**
- **Government-issued photo ID** — driver's license, passport, military ID, or TSA credential
- **Valid medical certificate** or **BasicMed** course completion certificate

### Critical Details
- All three must be in **physical possession** or **readily accessible** in the aircraft
- **Logbook is NOT required** in the aircraft — but must be produced upon request within a reasonable time
- An **expired driver's license** = cannot legally fly, even with a valid pilot certificate and medical

### Ramp Check Reality
- FAA inspectors can request to see all three documents
- "Readily accessible" means available during the flight — not back at home or in a flight bag outside the aircraft

required_knowledge_points.title: International Flight Document Requirements
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot flying to the Bahamas or Canada without the correct FCC documents faces international legal consequences and potential aircraft impoundment.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: For international flights, two additional documents are required beyond the Big Three. The pilot must hold a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit (FCC Form 605) — this is a lifetime permit requiring only an application and fee, no test. The aircraft must hold an Aircraft Radio Station License, valid for 10 years. These requirements come from 47 CFR Part 87, not FAA regulations. Domestic VFR flights within the United States do not require either document — aircraft are 'licensed by rule' for domestic operations.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### International Flights — Two Additional Documents Required
- **Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit** (FCC Form 605)
  - Required for the **pilot**
  - Lifetime permit — no test required, only application and fee
- **Aircraft Radio Station License**
  - Required for the **aircraft**
  - Valid for **10 years**

### Regulatory Source
- These requirements come from **47 CFR Part 87** — not FAA regulations (FCC jurisdiction)

### Domestic Flights
- Neither document is required for **domestic VFR flight** within the United States
- Aircraft are **licensed by rule** for domestic operations

lesson_overview:
## Medical Certificates (Classes & BasicMed)

Here's a question that catches more student pilots than almost any other: *when does your medical certificate expire?* The answer isn't on the face of the document — it depends on how old you were when the examiner signed it, which class you hold, and what privileges you're exercising. Let's untangle it.

**The three-class system.** The FAA issues three classes of medical certificate, each tied to a different level of pilot operations. A **First-Class** medical is required for Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) operations. A **Second-Class** is required for commercial operations — flying for hire. A **Third-Class** covers private, recreational, and student operations. Here's where most people get confused: the certificate class determines the initial duration, but the privilege you're *exercising* determines what's still valid. A First-Class medical doesn't disappear after its ATP window closes — it **steps down**. A 35-year-old pilot who gets a First-Class in January 2024 can exercise ATP privileges through January 2025, then that same piece of paper is valid for private pilot privileges for another four years. One physical, layered authority.

The duration math follows one rule: the FAA uses **calendar months**, and validity extends to the end of that month. A Second-Class issued on March 4th doesn't expire on March 4th of the following year — it's valid through March 31st. That month-end grace period is your friend, but only if you know it's there.

**The self-grounding rule: 14 CFR 61.53.** This is the regulation that catches the pilots who feel fine but *shouldn't be flying*. Even with a perfectly valid Third-Class medical in your wallet, you are legally prohibited from acting as PIC if you know of any medical condition that would make you unable to meet the standards for your certificate. The key word is *know* — not "have been told by the FAA." If you develop a severe kidney stone on a Sunday morning, you cannot fly to your $200 hamburger that afternoon, regardless of what the expiration date on your medical says. The same logic applies to medication: the FAA maintains a Do Not Fly list, and drugs like diphenhydramine (Benadryl) are on it. Whether you *feel* fine doesn't matter. The standard is based on the treatment, not your subjective assessment of your own fitness.

**The Big Three: what you need in the aircraft.** Under 14 CFR 61.3, you must have three documents in your physical possession or readily accessible in the cockpit: (1) your **pilot certificate** — the plastic card; paper certificates are no longer valid, (2) a **government-issued photo ID** — driver's license, passport, or military ID, and (3) your **medical certificate** or, if flying under BasicMed, your course completion certificate. Your logbook is not required to be in the aircraft, though you must be able to produce it on request within a reasonable time. One that surprises people: if your driver's license has expired, you legally cannot fly — even with a current pilot certificate and medical.

**BasicMed: the alternative path.** Since 2016, pilots have had a second route to medical certification that bypasses the Aviation Medical Examiner system entirely. Under 14 CFR Part 68, if you hold a valid U.S. driver's license and previously held any class of FAA medical after July 14, 2006, you can qualify under BasicMed. The requirements: a physical with any state-licensed MD or DO using the FAA's Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist (CMEC) every 48 months, and an online education course every 24 calendar months. The trade-off is a tighter operational envelope — no aircraft over 6,000 lbs or with more than 6 seats, no higher than 18,000 feet MSL, no faster than 250 knots.

**The checkride trap:** Applicants state the registration expires every three years (outdated) and that their medical expires on its face date (wrong — it's end of month). Know both.
